opening_note: October is San Diego's second summer. Some years the hottest week lands now, when the wind turns and blows in from the desert. But the harvest has moved inland: new dates, heavy pomegranates, the first guavas, and a squash that will sit on your counter until Thanksgiving. For the first time since spring, you can shop for the month instead of the week.
thesis: Keep the meal. Change the season.

bring_home.heading: This is what I'd bring home.
bring_home.cost_note: Around $30–40 for the seasonal basket, and half of it will still be good in three weeks. Proteins and pantry basics are separate. The ajvar wants four red bell peppers and one eggplant.

items.name: Kabocha squash
items.note: The sweetest squash there is. It keeps for months.

items.name: New-crop dates
items.note: Soft enough to dent. Last year's never are.

items.name: Guavas
items.note: Smell them before you see them. Buy the fragrant ones.

items.name: Arugula
items.note: The first greens since spring that aren't harsh.

items.name: Asian pears
items.note: Crisp like an apple, wet like a melon.

month_card.sub: What the desert and the valley send down.

field_notes.name: A new date isn't dried fruit.
field_notes.body: Most dates in the store were picked last fall and have been sitting since. The ones picked this fall are softer, glossier, and taste like caramel instead of candy — squeeze the box and they give. If you ever see yellow dates still on the branch, those are Barhis, eaten crunchy and fresh for a few weeks and nowhere else. Buy a branch.

field_notes.name: October is when peppers go in jars.
field_notes.body: Across the Balkans, autumn is ajvar season: red peppers are at their cheapest, and whole families roast them by the crate and cook them down into a relish that lasts the winter. You don't need a crate. Four peppers and one eggplant make a jar. It's the same impulse behind everything in this basket — buy it while it's here, and make it keep.

field_notes.name: Let the oven cut the kabocha.
field_notes.body: A kabocha is dense enough to be dangerous with a knife. Put it whole in a 400°F oven for ten minutes, or the microwave for three, and the skin softens enough to cut through safely. Don't peel it. Roasted, the skin goes tender and you eat all of it.

field_notes.name: October at the fish counter.
field_notes.body: Rockfish is the local fish that gets more reliable as the water cools: dozens of species, mild and firm, usually cheaper than anything flown in. Ask for it whole. A counter that sells it whole will scale and gut it for you, and a whole fish is easier to cook well than a fillet.

weekend_meal.name: Whole roasted rockfish, and the October salad.
weekend_meal.intro: One meal should feel like the reason you went shopping. In October, it's a whole local fish and a salad that only works this month: the first mild arugula, Asian pear, pomegranate, and new dates.
weekend_meal.card_line: Whole rockfish, arugula, Asian pear, pomegranate, dates, ajvar
ingredients: 1 whole rockfish, 2–3 lbs, scaled and gutted
1 lemon, sliced thin, plus another for the salad
A wedge of parmesan, for shaving
Ajvar and good bread, for the table
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: No whole fish at your counter? Two pounds of rockfish fillets work too — roast them for ten to twelve minutes instead.
weekend_meal.method: Heat the oven to 450°F. Pat the fish dry inside and out and cut three shallow slashes on each side, down to the bone. Rub it all over with olive oil, salt it well, inside and out, and tuck the lemon slices into the cavity. Roast on a sheet pan for 20 to 25 minutes, until the flesh at the thickest part is opaque and pulls easily from the bone. While it roasts, put the arugula, pear, pomegranate, and dates in a wide bowl, but don't dress them. At the table, add olive oil, a squeeze of lemon, and salt, toss, and shave parmesan over the top. Bring the fish out whole. Lift the top fillet off with a spoon, pull out the spine, and serve the bottom fillet. Ajvar and bread on the side.

drink.name: Barrio Logan Jamaica
drink.intro: One drink. It's still hot, and the pomegranates just came in.
drink.method: Cover a cup of dried hibiscus with four cups of cold water and leave it in the fridge overnight — cold-steeped, it comes out bright rather than bitter. Strain. Press the seeds from one pomegranate through a strainer and stir the juice in, with sugar to taste; start with a quarter cup and stop when it's tart-sweet, not sweet. Pour over ice with a squeeze of lime and a spoonful of whole seeds. The pitcher keeps four days.

local_ritual.label: San Diego ritual
local_ritual.name: Go to the desert.
local_ritual.description: Anza-Borrego is two hours east and unbearable until now. October is the first month it isn't. Go for a day, walk until it gets hot, and notice that the dates, the pomegranates, and the citrus coming next all grow somewhere that looks like this — dry, bright, and irrigated. The season in this basket comes from inland, not from the coast.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: The wind from the wrong direction.
one_thing_to_notice.body: A few times each fall the wind turns around and blows from the desert instead of the ocean. The air goes warm and very dry, the sky turns unusually clear, and from the coast you can suddenly see the mountains. It's why October can be hotter than August. When it happens, look east.
